blog.title: Paper Mills: The Dark Side of Academic Publishing
blog.excerpt: Somewhere in the published literature there is a paper discussing "bosom peril." Elsewhere there is one on "counterfeit consciousness." Neither phrase means anything, and both got past peer review, and once you know why, a fair amount of what is wrong with academic publishing falls into place.

research.title: Venus's Molten Fault Lines: How Magma Lubrication Shapes a Planet's Giant Cracks
research.excerpt: Venus gets called Earth's sister planet on the strength of its size, mass and bulk composition. The surface is a different matter: around 460 °C, no water anywhere, and a tectonic style that does not resemble ours.

research.title: Venus's Giant Eye: How Low-Angle Faults Reveal a Planet's Volcanic Past
research.excerpt: Coronae are among the strangest structures in the solar system: roughly circular features, hundreds to thousands of kilometres across, each ringed by a fractured annulus of ridges around a sunken middle. They are unique to Venus, and what makes them has been argued about for thirty years.

research.title: How Computer Models Helped Us Solve a 4-Billion-Year-Old Martian Mystery
research.excerpt: Open a topographic map of Mars and the first thing you notice is that the northern half sits about three kilometres lower than the southern half. That is the Martian dichotomy, and how it got there has been argued over for decades.

research.title: Peering Beneath Mars's Wrinkles: What Hidden Faults Tell Us About the Red Planet's Geology
research.excerpt: From orbit a wrinkle ridge is a gentle bump. What makes it is a fault, and the fault is underground, which is the awkward part: we cannot drill into Mars to look at it.
